context: civil-pavement-led · workshop & fuelling/EV-charging systems overlay the paved yard

brief.intro: New to this project type? A bus depot or transport hub is fundamentally a large paved yard for bus circulation, parking and washing, with a smaller building block — maintenance workshops, fuelling or EV-charging infrastructure, and admin — sitting inside it. Progress is measured across two very different fronts at once: hectares of heavy-duty pavement and drainage across the yard, and a workshop/systems fit-out with real MEP content (workshop pits and lifts, fuelling or EV-charging equipment, wash-bay water recycling). Its acceptance test is entirely operational — a bus has to be able to fuel or charge, wash and be serviced end-to-end before handover, not just look complete.

scope.name: Bus-wash facility

scope.name: Testing & commissioning
scope.desc: Workshop equipment, fuelling/EV-charging, and wash & drainage-interceptor commissioning.

glossary.plain: the heavy-duty paved yard designed for repeated bus loading, not ordinary car-park pavement.
a drainage chamber that traps fuel/oil before yard water reaches the storm system.
an in-ground or hydraulic platform letting mechanics work underneath a bus.
the civil base and the high-capacity electrical supply a bus charger needs — often larger than the rest of the depot's normal load.

must_get_right: The paved yard (circulation, parking, drainage) is the largest-quantity item on the job — get the pavement design and interceptor drainage right before workshop and systems fit-out compete for the same space.
Fuelling or EV-charging infrastructure usually needs a much larger utility/power feed than the rest of the depot combined — start that utility application early; it can dominate the critical path.
Treat operational commissioning (a bus actually fuels or charges, washes and is serviced end-to-end) as the real acceptance test, not practical completion of the buildings.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are coded by yard zone/chainage so pavement progress is tracked by area alongside the building-block activities. Total float is kept ≥ 0 in the baseline.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Earthworks and pavement run an extended, weather-dependent calendar (asphalt paving further restricted by minimum ambient/surface temperature); workshop and admin structure/MEP run a standard calendar; fuelling/EV-charging installation and commissioning follows the utility provider's own outage/connection windows.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path usually runs the high-capacity utility feed application/approval (for EV-charging or bulk fuel supply) in parallel with bulk earthworks and pavement, converging at fuelling/EV-charging equipment installation → systems integration → operational commissioning → handover. Workshop and admin structure typically have float relative to the pavement and utility-feed fronts.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Design and approvals are frozen per zone; the utility company has confirmed capacity and connection date for the high-capacity feed; borrow/spoil arrangements are secured for bulk earthworks; a single mobilisation; if the depot is operational during works, phased handover of yard zones is coordinated with operations. Any change to these invalidates the baseline dates.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The schedule is driven by the fuelling/EV-charging supply chain and the utility feed. The following are tracked as milestones and drive the network:

rows: EV charger units / transformer upgrade (or fuel tanks & dispensers)

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Haul-road access and asphalt-plant capacity govern pavement pace; the utility company's own programme for the high-capacity feed is a hard external constraint; if buses continue to operate from the depot during works, phased lane and bay closures limit which zones can be worked at once.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: delay to the high-capacity utility feed, weather stopping earthworks or paving, and fuel-system/EV-charging permitting delays. Schedule contingency is held around the utility-feed milestone and again ahead of operational commissioning, rather than spread thinly across the network.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
